candidates.attacker_control: The attacker supplies the serialized byte stream that the integrating application deserializes as a `DiskFileItem` (or subclass such as `DefaultFileItem`), i.e. fully controls all serialized fields: repository path, sizeThreshold, cachedContent bytes, dfosFile path, headers, field/file names. Normal HTTP multipart handling does not pass through `readObject`; the attack requires an application sink that deserializes untrusted data into these types (distributed cache/session replication, message queue, RMI/HTTP object endpoint, stored upload blobs).
candidates.counterevidence_checked: (1) `repository` may legitimately be null: the code then falls back to `java.io.tmpdir`, so null alone is not evidence of a missing control, but a non-null deserialized path is used verbatim. (2) Normal upload flow is constrained: `DiskFileItemFactory.createItem` passes the factory-configured repository, so the multipart request path is not directly affected; the issue is confined to the deserialization path. (3) No `readObject` caller exists in this snapshot, so this cannot be triggered via `FileUploadBase`/`ServletFileUpload` alone; an application deserialization sink is required. (4) `fileName` handling is independently hardened (`Streams.checkFileName`, `InvalidFileNameException`), so path traversal via the file name is not the mechanism. (5) Searched the whole tree for `isDirectory` and `InvalidObjectException`: zero hits, supporting that no repository validation is implemented.
candidates.impact: During deserialization the application writes fully attacker-controlled content into an attacker-chosen directory under a fixed-format temporary name (`upload_<JVM-random-UID>_<counter>.tmp`), or reads an attacker-named `dfosFile` path and copies its contents into that directory. Impact depends on the deployment: unintended/overwriting file creation outside the configured repository, planting content in directories that are scanned/executed or subsequently served, and local-file content being exfiltrated into application-visible storage. Because the filename prefix/extension is fixed and the UID is a per-JVM random value, direct targeting of a pre-existing filename is limited, which tempers severity.
candidates.prerequisites: An application deserializes attacker-influenced data into `org.apache.commons.fileupload.disk.DiskFileItem`; the deserialized `sizeThreshold` is set low enough (or the content large enough) that `DeferredFileOutputStream` actually spills to disk (otherwise content remains in memory); the process identity has write permission on the attacker-chosen directory. No library API inside this snapshot calls `readObject`, so this is not reachable through `ServletFileUpload.parseRequest` alone.
candidates.root_cause: `DiskFileItem` is Serializable (`FileItem extends Serializable`) and serializes its `repository` File field, `sizeThreshold`, `cachedContent` and `dfosFile`. `readObject` calls `in.defaultReadObject()` and then unconditionally opens an output stream via `getOutputStream()` -> `getTempFile()`, which builds `new File(repository, "upload_<UID>_<counter>.tmp")` from the deserialized `repository` and writes the deserialized `cachedContent` (or copies from the deserialized `dfosFile` path) into it. There is no validation that the deserialized repository is a legitimate/valid directory: `isDirectory`/`InvalidObjectException` do not appear anywhere in the snapshot, and `DiskFileItem` imports no validation API. This directly contradicts the repository's own changelog entry for 1.3.1, which states this hardening was made. The permanent `UID`/counter file naming and the `fileName` sanitization do not constrain the attacker-chosen repository directory or the written bytes.
candidates.title: DiskFileItem deserialization uses attacker-controlled repository/content without validation (missing repository check)
candidates.trace: ObjectInputStream.readObject -> DiskFileItem.readObject (line 654) -> in.defaultReadObject() restores repository/cachedContent/sizeThreshold/dfosFile -> getOutputStream() (line 525) -> getTempFile() (line 578) builds File(repository != null ? repository : java.io.tmpdir, format("upload_%s_%s.tmp", UID, getUniqueId())) -> DeferredFileOutputStream(sizeThreshold, outputFile) -> if cachedContent != null output.write(cachedContent) (line 661), else copy from deserialized dfosFile then delete it (lines 663-666) -> output.close() flushes the attacker-influenced bytes into the attacker-chosen directory.
candidates.unverified: Not runtime-confirmed and no test sources exist in this snapshot to observe behavior. The strength of the 'missing intended fix' claim rests on the changelog text (src/changes/changes.xml lines 46-51) rather than on a diff against the upstream fixed revision; the exact form the upstream check took is inferred. Whether a concrete, reachable deserialization sink exists in a consuming application is unknown from this snapshot, so attacker control is conditional on the integrating application.
candidates.weakness_type: Deserialization of untrusted data leading to arbitrary file write (CWE-502/CWE-73)

coverage_summary: Source scope: 63 files, all model-visible (no binaries, symlinks, or sensitive-name exclusions). I read in full: MultipartStream, DiskFileItem, DiskFileItemFactory, DefaultFileItem, DefaultFileItemFactory, ParameterParser, MimeUtility, Base64Decoder, QuotedPrintableDecoder, Streams, LimitedInputStream, FileItemHeadersImpl, ServletRequestContext, FileCleanerCleanup, RELEASE-NOTES.txt, pom.xml (top), build.properties, and the changes.xml security sections. I read substantial portions of FileUploadBase (lines 1-1250 of 1474: iterator, boundary/file-name/header parsing, size limits, exception plumbing) and partial sections of changelog tail. I did not inspect in detail: ServletFileUpload, PortletFileUpload, PortletRequestContext, DiskFileUpload, FileUpload, FileItem/FileItemStream/FileItemIterator/FileItemFactory/FileItemHeaders interfaces, RequestContext, UploadContext, ProgressListener, Closeable, the exception classes in FileUploadBase lines 1250-1474, package-info files, build.xml/build-gump.xml/gump.xml, checkstyle configs, and src/site documentation. The P1 relation index covers all 63 files (0 missing) with 445 symbols/686 edges/calls 530; I used it only for navigation (its 12 'facts' are name-based hints, and it performs no control/data-flow, reachability, or exploitability analysis). No tests exist in the snapshot and nothing was compiled or executed.
limitations: No test sources in the snapshot and no build/test execution, so all conclusions are static source readings, not runtime-confirmed behavior.
The relation index is syntactic/navigation-only and cannot prove reachability or data flow; no scanner or ground-truth data was consulted.

The candidate's 'missing security control' conclusion is derived from repository documentation (changes.xml 46-51) plus the absence of validation in DiskFileItem; the exact upstream fixed form of that control is inferred, not verified against a diff.
Exploitability of the DiskFileItem finding depends on an application-side deserialization sink that is outside this snapshot; the library's own multipart handling path does not call readObject.
I did not fully audit FileUploadBase lines 1250-1474, the servlet/portlet adapters, the interfaces, build files, or site documentation, so additional issues there cannot be ruled out.

The MultipartStream CPU-spin lead depends on servlet container input-stream behavior for zero-length reads (standard InputStream contract says 0, but the container implementation is outside the snapshot).

rejected_leads.lead: MultipartStream.ItemInputStream.makeAvailable() (src/main/java/org/apache/commons/fileupload/MultipartStream.java lines 983-1017): the unbounded `for(;;)` loop can fail to make progress when the buffer is full (`tail == bufSize`) and no separator is found because the boundary token is longer than the buffer (`boundaryLength > bufSize`, default bufSize 4096; getBoundary/FileUploadBase lines 419-436 and 988-994 impose no boundary length limit). It then repeatedly calls input.read(buffer, bufSize, 0), which per InputStream contract returns 0, spinning at 100% CPU. This looks like a genuine remotely-triggerable DoS with only a crafted Content-Type boundary, but I could not tie it to the snapshot's intended missing control (the changelog describes only the disk-item validation), and the buffer/boundary relationship could reflect a later upstream fix; kept out of the candidate list under the one-candidate cap.
rejected_leads.reason: Plausible remote DoS, but weaker repository-internal evidence than the changelog-corroborated missing repository validation; primary uncertainty is whether a conforming servlet input stream returns 0 (vs blocking/throwing) for a zero-length read, which I cannot confirm statically.

rejected_leads.lead: Unbounded number of multipart parts: FileUploadBase has sizeMax/fileSizeMax limits but no per-request part-count limit (`findNextItem`, lines 1007-1073; parseRequest lines 329-374), so a request with many small parts consumes CPU/disk proportional to part count.
rejected_leads.reason: Real hardening gap, but a configuration-level resource limitation rather than a distinct memory-safety or injection flaw in this snapshot's own logic; no attacker-controlled unbounded loop/overflow could be established from source alone.

rejected_leads.lead: MimeUtility / Base64Decoder / QuotedPrintableDecoder / ParameterParser decoding paths reviewed (decodeText whitespace handling, padding validation, hex escape bounds, token parsing): no concrete memory corruption, infinite loop, or injection defect was found in source.
rejected_leads.reason: No evidence of a distinct exploitable flaw; padding/truncation errors are converted to IOExceptions.

rejected_leads.lead: Default repository is java.io.tmpdir with predictable names (CVE-2013-0248-style local TOUTOC attack).
rejected_leads.reason: Already documented and mitigated in the snapshot: DiskFileItemFactory and DiskFileUpload javadoc explicitly warn and require setRepository for untrusted-local-user environments, so this is a documented configuration requirement, not an unaddressed code defect.

summary: Reviewed the 63-file Apache Commons FileUpload snapshot (version 1.4-SNAPSHOT per pom.xml, unreleased 1.3.1 section in changes.xml). The strongest distinct issue found is on the serialization path of the disk-backed file item: `DiskFileItem.readObject()` restores attacker-influenced fields (repository, sizeThreshold, cachedContent, dfosFile) and then performs a file write into the restored repository directory without any validation, even though the project's own changelog records that this validation ("ensure that the repository location, if any, is a valid one") was the intended security fix. No such check exists anywhere in the tree. The evidence is a missing-control finding corroborated by repository documentation plus the concrete code path; it was not runtime-confirmed and its exploitability depends on an application-side deserialization sink. A second plausible issue (parser CPU spin with an over-long multipart boundary) is recorded as an unconfirmed rejected lead, per the one-candidate cap.
